transcript.text: Hi! Could you pull which customers spent less this quarter than last quarter? I'm thinking of sending them something to bring them back, maybe a 15% coupon. The sales export is attached. [shares sales.csv]

Thanks, that's clear: you want the list of customers whose spend dropped from last quarter to this one, so you can decide whether a 15% coupon is worth sending them. Your sales export has 2,020 orders with a customer_id, an order date, an amount and a status, so I can compute each customer's spend per quarter. One thing changes how I build the list: who do you want the coupon to reach? Do you mean customers who have gone quiet and not ordered at all this quarter, or also customers who still buy but spend a bit less? And does any drop count, or only a meaningful one?

Good question, and thanks for asking before building anything. I want the customers who are slipping but haven't fully left yet. So I'd include people who still buy but spent clearly less this quarter than last, and people who ordered last quarter and haven't ordered at all this quarter. I'd leave out anyone whose spend is flat or up, since they'd probably buy anyway, and I'd probably leave out customers who have been gone for a long time, since a 15% coupon is unlikely to bring them back. I'm not sure what counts as a meaningful drop. Maybe a fall of 30% or more, or something you'd suggest? Since I can only send to 1,000 people, I'd like a ranked list so I can take the top 1,000. Could you rank by how much their spend fell, or by something that also reflects how valuable they were before the drop? I can do the pivot work in Excel, but I haven't built a scoring model before, so keep the method simple enough that I can explain it to the marketing manager, who approves the list. Also, could we hold back a random group of eligible customers from the coupon, so we can check later whether the coupon actually helped?

Your plan is clear, so I've started building the ranked win-back list. Here is the rule I'm using. It needs no scoring model, and you can rebuild it in Excel as a pivot. - **Spend:** I add up `amount` on orders with status "paid" only. The export has 1,733 paid, 188 refunded and 99 cancelled orders. A refunded or cancelled order isn't money the customer spent. - **Quarters:** I compare the last two full calendar quarters in the export. The result will state the exact dates. Your `order_date` column converts to dates cleanly. - **Who qualifies:** Customers who spent in the earlier quarter and whose spend this quarter is at least 30% lower, including customers at zero. That is the cut-off you suggested, and it ignores normal ups and downs. Customers who didn't buy in the earlier quarter are left out, so people who left long ago are excluded without a separate rule. Flat or higher spenders are excluded too. - **Ranking:** By dollars lost, which is last quarter's spend minus this quarter's. A big spender who fell a lot ranks above a small spender who fell by a larger percentage, so value is built in. The marketing manager can check it with one subtraction. - **Holdout:** I'll set aside a random share of the customers who would have been mailed and leave them out of the coupon. After the send, you compare their spending with the coupon group's. Drawing them from the mailing group means the two groups are like for like. I'll show you how many customers that is, and you can make it bigger or smaller. Only 938 customers in the whole export have a paid order, so far fewer than 1,000 may qualify. If so, the 1,000 limit won't apply and everyone eligible, minus the holdout, gets the coupon. You'll get the list as a file with the quarter dates, the number who qualify and each customer's spend in both quarters. It will also show which customers are in the holdout. If the counts look too big or too small, we can change the 30% cut-off or the holdout size and rerun it.

transcript.text: quick q: churn with 3% positives, should i report PR-AUC or ROC-AUC to my manager, and why? no data work, just the answer

Report PR-AUC as your headline number. If your manager expects to see ROC-AUC, put it next to PR-AUC as a secondary figure. ROC-AUC can look good when the model isn't. It is built on the false positive rate, and that rate is measured against the large majority of customers who don't churn. A model can flag many non-churners and still have a small false positive rate. ROC-AUC can then look strong even though most of the people you'd contact are not going to leave. PR-AUC measures what your retention team deals with. It tracks precision (of the people we flag, how many really churn) against recall (of the people who churn, how many we catch). It ignores the large pool of easy true negatives. When you present it:
- **Give the baseline.** A model with no skill has a PR-AUC equal to the churn rate, which for you is the 3% you mentioned. Show your model's PR-AUC next to that figure so your manager can see how much better than chance it is. - **Add one business-level figure.** For example: "if we contact the top slice of customers by risk, this share of them churn, and we reach this share of all churners." A manager can act on that more easily than on any AUC. - **Don't compare PR-AUC across datasets with different churn rates.** It depends on the base rate. ROC-AUC does not. - **Compute both on held-out data.** Use data the model never trained on. That's the full answer, and I haven't done any work on your data. If you later want to measure a real model this way, share the table and we can do it then.

I can't tell whether nobody signed up that year or the date filter didn't match, so I'm not reading anything into it. - I have no year-by-year numbers, so I can't say yet whether tenure_months looks like a snapshot. **Run these on your side (Postgres syntax)**

1. Count and mean tenure by signup year and churn:
```sql
SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM signup_date) AS signup_year,
       churned_next_month,
       COUNT(*) AS n,
       AVG(tenure_months) AS mean_tenure,
       MIN(tenure_months) AS min_tenure,
       MAX(tenure_months) AS max_tenure
FROM customers
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;
```

2. The direct snapshot test, which is the implied reference date (signup_date + tenure_months) by churn group:
```sql
SELECT churned_next_month,
       COUNT(*) AS n,
       MIN(d) AS earliest,
       MAX(d) AS latest,
       COUNT(DISTINCT DATE_TRUNC('month', d)) AS distinct_months
FROM (SELECT churned_next_month,
             signup_date + tenure_months * INTERVAL '1 month' AS d
      FROM customers) t
GROUP BY 1;
```
